title: Dennis Lillee's aluminium bat
hook: A fast bowler walked out to bat with a metal bat, and cricket rewrote its laws.
peek: In a 1979 Test match in Perth, the Australian fast bowler Dennis Lillee came out to bat with a bat made of aluminium. The row that followed stopped play, and cricket's laws were soon changed to say bats must be wooden.
lede: In December 1979, at the WACA ground in Perth, Australia's Dennis Lillee walked out against England carrying a bat made of aluminium. At the time, the laws of cricket did not actually say what a bat had to be made of. Within minutes the game had stopped for an argument, and within months the rules had been rewritten.

bullets.text: The bat was made by a company run by a friend of Lillee's, and was meant as a cheap alternative to willow for schools and developing cricket countries. Lillee had already used it in a Test against the West Indies weeks earlier without fuss.

England's captain, Mike Brearley, objected that the metal was damaging the ball. Lillee's own captain, Greg Chappell, also thought a wooden bat would hit better. After a delay of about ten minutes, Lillee flung the bat away and carried on with willow.
Cricket's lawmakers, the MCC, then amended the laws in 1980 to state that the blade of a bat must be made of wood. That rule still stands, which is why every professional bat today is willow.
The players later signed the aluminium bat, and Brearley is said to have added a dry note wishing it good luck with the sales. It became one of cricket's best-known oddities.
